1.title: Introduction to Electrical Energy and DC Circuits
1.scope_note: All 26 Chapter 1 review questions have source-backed study solutions. Short Q15–Q16 and Essay Q10 are retained as supporting transient-circuit material outside current R25 Unit I, using newly supplied textbook pp.62–69.

questions.question: List the advantages of electrical energy over other forms of energy.

bullets: It is convenient because it can be converted readily into light, heat, cooling and mechanical motion.
It is easily controllable: electrically operated equipment can be started, stopped and regulated conveniently.
It is economical and suitable for domestic, commercial and industrial loads.
It is clean at the point of use because utilisation itself does not produce smoke or fumes.
It can be transmitted from the generating location to distant load centres.

questions.question: Define an electric generator and an electric motor.

bullets: Electric generator: an electrical machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
Electric motor: an electrical machine that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.

questions.question: What is an electric circuit?

paragraphs: An electric circuit is an interconnection of electrical elements arranged so that at least one closed conducting path exists for current. A basic circuit contains a source, load, connecting conductors and usually a control such as a switch.

questions.question: Compare electric and magnetic circuits.

paragraphs: Electric and magnetic circuits can be treated as analogous systems.

rows: MMF = NI (ampere-turns) provides the driving force
Current I is the through quantity
Magnetic flux Φ is the corresponding through quantity
For a resistive circuit, I = V/R
For a magnetic circuit, Φ = MMF/Reluctance

questions.question: Name the basic circuit parameters.

paragraphs: The three basic passive circuit parameters are resistance (R), inductance (L) and capacitance (C).

questions.question: Differentiate between resistance and inductance.

rows: Opposes current and dissipates absorbed electrical energy mainly as heat.
Opposes change in current and stores energy in a magnetic field.
For a linear resistor: v = Ri.
For an ideal inductor: v = L·di/dt.
Power is dissipated: p = i²R = v²/R.

questions.question: How does an inductor behave in a DC circuit?

paragraphs: For steady DC, current is constant, so di/dt = 0. Hence vL = L·di/dt = 0. An ideal inductor therefore behaves as a short circuit after DC steady state has been reached.
answer.note: The switching transient itself is not part of the current R25 Unit I source set.

questions.question: Write the expression for energy stored in a capacitor.

paragraphs: Thus the energy stored in the electric field of a capacitor is one-half of C times the square of the capacitor voltage.

questions.question: How does a capacitor behave in a DC circuit?

paragraphs: For steady DC, capacitor voltage is constant, so dv/dt = 0. Hence iC = C·dv/dt = 0. An ideal capacitor therefore behaves as an open circuit in DC steady state.
answer.note: The charging/discharging transient is outside the current R25 Unit I source set.

questions.question: Differentiate between independent and dependent voltage sources.

rows: Its specified voltage is set independently of other circuit variables.
Its voltage is controlled by another voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit.
Ideal source maintains the prescribed terminal voltage regardless of the current demanded by the connected circuit.
Its value changes according to its controlling-variable relationship, such as v = μvₓ or v = riₓ.

questions.question: Describe the V–I characteristics of ideal voltage and current sources.

bullets: Ideal voltage source: terminal voltage remains fixed at Vₛ while current may take whatever value the external circuit requires. Its characteristic is therefore a constant-voltage line.
Ideal current source: source current remains fixed at Iₛ while terminal voltage may take whatever value the external circuit requires. Its characteristic is therefore a constant-current line.

questions.question: Show the equivalent circuits of practical voltage and current sources.

bullets: Practical voltage source: an ideal voltage source Vₛ in series with an internal resistance Rₛ.
Practical current source: an ideal current source Iₛ in parallel with an internal resistance Rₛ.
answer.note: These two practical-source forms are also the pair used in source transformation.

questions.question: For the 48 V source with 25 Ω series resistance in Fig. 1.73, find the equivalent current source.

steps: Use source transformation: Iₛ = Vₛ/Rₛ.
Keep the same resistance value, 25 Ω, but place it in parallel with the current source.
answer.result: Equivalent source: 1.92 A current source in parallel with 25 Ω.

figures.alt: Circuit with a 48 volt ideal voltage source in series with a 25 ohm resistance between output terminals a and b, for conversion to an equivalent current source.
figures.caption: Fig. 1.73 · Voltage-source circuit for source transformation

questions.question: State KCL and KVL.

bullets: Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL): the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero; equivalently, total current entering a node equals total current leaving it.
Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL): the algebraic sum of all voltage rises and drops around any closed loop is zero.

questions.question: Define transient state.

paragraphs: Transient state is the transition interval after a circuit change, such as switching, during which its currents and voltages move from their previous conditions toward the new steady state.
answer.note: Supporting textbook material outside current R25 Unit I; now source-backed by the newly supplied pp.62–69.

questions.question: Write the expression for the time constant of an RC network.

paragraphs: For a first-order series RC circuit the time constant is \(\tau=RC\) seconds. More generally, \(R\) is the resistance seen by the capacitor with independent sources suppressed.
answer.note: Supporting textbook material outside current R25 Unit I; now source-backed by the newly supplied pp.62–69.

questions.question: Explain the role of electrical energy in modern life.

paragraphs: Electrical energy is one of the most useful forms of energy in modern society because it can be generated from many primary energy sources, transmitted to the place of use, controlled conveniently and converted into the form of energy required by the load.

Its importance is seen not only in homes but also in commerce, industry, transport, communication, medicine, scientific work and computing. The prescribed text also connects electrical-energy use with economic activity and quality of life.
bullets: Convenience: electrical energy can be converted readily into light, heat, cooling and mechanical rotation.

Easy control and flexibility: electrical equipment can be started, stopped and regulated conveniently; an electric motor, for example, can be controlled electrically without handling the mechanical load directly.
Economy: electricity is suitable for domestic, commercial and industrial service and is economical for a wide range of loads.
Clean point of use: electrical utilisation itself does not produce smoke, fumes or poisonous gases at the load, giving cleaner working conditions than direct combustion at the point of use.
Easy transmission: electrical energy can be generated where resources are available and transmitted efficiently to distant load centres.
Domestic and commercial applications include lighting, heating, cooling, refrigeration, appliances, computers, electronics and office equipment.
Industrial applications include motor drives, process and production equipment, lighting, computers and building services such as heating, cooling and ventilation.
Transport and communication depend strongly on electricity: electric trains, battery vehicles, radio, television and related systems are examples.
Medicine and science use electrically powered equipment such as X-ray and ECG systems, while modern computers, robots and communication infrastructure depend fundamentally on electrical power.
Electric vehicles and renewable-energy systems are growing applications; solar, wind and hydel resources can be converted into electrical energy for useful consumption.
paragraphs_after: Thus electrical energy is not merely another form of energy: it is the common intermediate form that links generation, transmission and a very large variety of useful end applications. Its controllability, transmissibility and ease of conversion make it central to modern engineering and daily life.
answer.note: For a 6-mark answer, write a short introduction, any five advantages, several modern applications, and a one-line conclusion.

questions.question: With the help of a single-line diagram, explain electrical power generation, transmission and utilization.

answer.diagram: Primary energy / mechanical energy → Generating system (prime mover + generator) → Electrical energy → Transmission → Load centre → Distribution → Utilisation loads
paragraphs: Electrical power generation means converting an available form of energy into electrical energy. Natural energy may be available as heat, chemical, solar, wind, water or mechanical energy. In conventional generating stations, a prime mover supplies mechanical energy to a generator, and the generator converts that mechanical energy into electrical energy.

Generating stations are generally located according to the availability of the primary resource, whereas consumers may be far away. The generated electrical power therefore has to be carried from the generating station to the load centre through a transmission system.
steps: Generation: a primary source supplies energy. In a conventional plant the prime mover produces mechanical power and drives the generator.
Energy conversion in the generator: mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy.
Transmission: bulk electrical power is carried over conductors from the generating station towards the load centres.
Distribution: at the receiving/load centre, the power is distributed through the distribution system to individual consumers.
Utilisation: consumers convert the received electrical energy into the required useful effect—lighting, heating, cooling, computing, communication or mechanical output.
Motive loads: many practical loads ultimately require mechanical motion; an electric motor performs the reverse conversion of a generator, converting electrical energy into mechanical energy.
paragraphs_after: The complete chain consisting of generation, transmission, distribution and utilisation is called an electrical power system. In energy-conversion terms, the generator is a mechanical-to-electrical converter, while the motor is an electrical-to-mechanical converter.
answer.note: In the examination, draw the single-line block diagram first and then explain each block in order.

questions.question: Discuss the behavior of (a) inductance and (b) capacitance when placed in electrical circuits.

paragraphs: Inductance and capacitance are energy-storage parameters. Unlike an ideal resistor, they are dynamic elements: their present terminal behaviour depends on the rate of change of current or voltage and therefore carries memory of the previous state.

rows: A current-carrying coil establishes magnetic flux. For a linear inductor, flux linkage is proportional to current.
A capacitor consists of conducting plates separated by an insulating dielectric; equal and opposite charge is stored on the plates.
A finite voltage cannot change ideal-inductor current instantaneously; inductor current is continuous.
A finite current cannot change ideal-capacitor voltage instantaneously; capacitor voltage is continuous.
The induced emf opposes the change in current that produces it (Lenz-law interpretation).
Current flows while the capacitor voltage is changing; charge accumulation creates the electric field between the plates.
Under steady DC, di/dt = 0, so v_L = 0 and an ideal inductor behaves as a short circuit.
Under steady DC, dv/dt = 0, so i_C = 0 and an ideal capacitor behaves as an open circuit.

paragraphs_after: The integral relations show why both elements are said to have memory: their current or voltage at a later time contains the initial value. This distinction from a resistor is important whenever a circuit changes with time.

For the present R25 Unit I, the required emphasis is on the element relations, stored energy and steady-DC behaviour. Detailed RL/RC switching transients lie outside the supplied R25 Unit-I source set.

questions.question: What are the different types of dependent sources? Give their controlling relations and characteristics.

paragraphs: A dependent or controlled source is a source whose output voltage or current is determined by another voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit. It is represented by a diamond-shaped source symbol, distinguishing it from the circular symbol normally used for an independent source.
Controlled sources are very useful as linear models of more complicated circuits. The Unit-I lectures use an amplifier as an example of a system that can be represented by a controlled source.

rows: An input/control voltage determines the output voltage.
An input/control voltage determines the output current.
A sensed/control current determines the output voltage.
A sensed/control current determines the output current.

bullets: The controlling quantity and the output quantity may be in different parts of the circuit.
For a voltage-controlled source, the controlling variable is a voltage measured between specified nodes.
For a current-controlled source, the controlling variable is a branch current; the lecture representation uses a sensing short-circuit branch to define that current.
With constant proportionality factors μ, g, r or β, the controlled-source relation is linear, so the source can participate in linear-circuit analysis and superposition.
A dependent source is not turned off merely because independent sources are deactivated; it remains active as long as its controlling variable exists.
paragraphs_after: Hence the four dependent sources arise from the four possible combinations of input/control variable (voltage or current) and output variable (voltage or current). Remembering this 2 × 2 classification makes the four types easy to reconstruct in an examination.

questions.question: Explain the procedure for converting a current source into its equivalent voltage source.

paragraphs: A practical current source consists of an ideal current source I_s in parallel with a resistance R. It can be replaced, at the same pair of external terminals, by an equivalent practical voltage source consisting of an ideal voltage source V_s in series with the same resistance R.
steps: Identify the current-source value I_s and the resistance R connected directly in parallel with it.
Retain exactly the same resistance value R in the transformed circuit, but place it in series with the voltage source.
Calculate the equivalent voltage-source value from V_s = I_sR.
Choose the voltage polarity so that the open-circuit terminal voltage has the same polarity as that produced by the original current source.
Reconnect the external load to the same two terminals. The load voltage and load current will be the same for both source representations.
paragraphs_after: Why the transformation works: with the load removed, the current source drives I_s through R, giving an open-circuit terminal voltage V_oc = I_sR. In the voltage-source form, the open-circuit terminal voltage is V_s, so choosing V_s = I_sR makes the two open-circuit voltages equal. With the terminals shorted, the voltage-source form supplies I_sc = V_s/R = I_s, which is also the short-circuit current of the original current-source form. Thus the two networks have the same terminal behaviour.
The reverse transformation follows immediately: a voltage source V_s in series with R is equivalent to a current source I_s = V_s/R in parallel with the same R.
answer.note: Source transformation gives terminal equivalence. Internal branch voltages and currents inside the two source representations need not be identical.

questions.question: Explain Kirchhoff’s laws with examples.

paragraphs: Kirchhoff’s laws are general laws for currents at a node and voltages around a closed loop. They are not tied to a particular resistor or source; they are used to write circuit equations for an interconnected network.
equations: KVL: Σv = 0 around a closed loop
bullets: Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL): the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero. Equivalently, total current entering a node equals total current leaving it. This expresses conservation of electric charge.
A convenient sign convention is to take currents entering the node as positive and currents leaving as negative, or vice versa. Either convention gives the same physical result if used consistently.
Example of KCL: if 2 A and 3 A enter a node and only one branch leaves, the leaving current must be 5 A, because 2 + 3 − 5 = 0.

Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL): as a loop is traversed once and returns to the starting node, the algebraic sum of all voltage rises and voltage drops is zero. This is the circuit form of conservation of energy.
For KVL, first choose a loop direction. Treat each encountered voltage as a rise or a drop according to its marked polarity, write the algebraic sum, and set it equal to zero.
Example of KVL: a 10 V rise followed by drops of 4 V and 6 V gives +10 − 4 − 6 = 0.
paragraphs_after: KCL is applied at nodes; KVL is applied around closed loops. Together with the voltage-current relations of the elements, these laws provide the basic equations from which unknown branch currents and voltages are obtained.

The Unit-I lecture also notes the usual lumped-circuit assumption behind KVL: the loop should not be linked by a significant time-varying magnetic field. This assumption is satisfied for the ordinary circuit problems treated here.
answer.note: In an exam answer, state each law, write its equation, mention the physical conservation principle, and give one small signed example.

questions.question: Using Kirchhoff’s laws, find the current through the 3 Ω resistor in Fig. 1.74.

paragraphs: Use the polarities shown in Fig. 1.74 and write KCL equations for the unknown upper nodes. Take the bottom conductor as the reference node (0 V). The 12 V source fixes the left upper node at +12 V. Let the top-centre node be V and the top-right node be V_r. Because the 8 V source in the centre branch has its positive terminal below as drawn, the node immediately above the 3 Ω resistor is V + 8.
steps: From the second equation, solve the relationship between V_r and V, then substitute it into the first KCL equation.
Solving the two simultaneous equations gives V ≈ −2.80 V and V_r ≈ −1.53 V.
The voltage across the 3 Ω resistor, measured from its upper end to the reference node, is V + 8 ≈ 5.20 V.
Therefore I_3Ω = (V + 8)/3 ≈ 1.734 A.
answer.result: Current through the 3 Ω resistor ≈ 1.73 A downward through the middle branch.
answer.book_check: Printed answer: 1.736 A; direct calculation from the figure gives about 1.734 A, consistent with rounding.
answer.note: A complete 6-mark numerical answer should show the reference node, variable definitions, both Kirchhoff equations, the simultaneous-equation solution and the final current with direction.

figures.alt: Kirchhoff-law circuit with a 12 volt source on the left, an 8 volt source and 3 ohm resistor in the middle branch, 10 and 5 ohm top resistors, and a 6 ohm right-hand resistor.
figures.caption: Fig. 1.74 · Circuit for finding the current through the 3 Ω resistor

questions.question: Using Star–Delta transformation, find the source current for the circuit in Fig. 1.75.

paragraphs: The network in Fig. 1.75 is not immediately reducible by ordinary series/parallel combinations because the right-hand 2 Ω, 4 Ω and 10 Ω resistors form a Δ. Convert that Δ into its equivalent star; after the conversion, the remaining network becomes series-parallel.
equations: For Δ → Y: R_a = (product of the two Δ arms touching terminal a)/(sum of all three Δ arms)
steps: Star arm toward the top node = (2×4)/16 = 0.5 Ω.
Star arm toward the bottom node = (2×10)/16 = 1.25 Ω.
Star arm toward the right/source terminal = (4×10)/16 = 2.5 Ω.
The upper left path becomes 8 + 0.5 = 8.5 Ω.
The lower left path becomes 6 + 1.25 = 7.25 Ω.
These two paths are in parallel: R_p = (8.5×7.25)/(8.5+7.25) ≈ 3.913 Ω.
The 2.5 Ω star arm is then in series with this parallel equivalent: R_eq = 3.913 + 2.5 ≈ 6.413 Ω.
Source current I = 18/R_eq = 18/6.413 ≈ 2.807 A.
answer.note: The key scoring step is the correct Δ-to-Y conversion followed by a clearly redrawn series-parallel equivalent.

figures.alt: Bridge resistor network supplied by an 18 volt source, with 8 and 6 ohm left branches, 4 and 10 ohm right branches, and a 2 ohm central branch for Star–Delta transformation.
figures.caption: Fig. 1.75 · Bridge network for Star–Delta transformation

questions.question: State and explain the Superposition theorem.

paragraphs: Superposition theorem applies to linear circuits containing more than one independent source. It allows the effect of the sources to be separated, one source at a time, and then recombined algebraically.

Statement: in a linear circuit, the voltage across or current through any chosen element with all independent sources acting together equals the algebraic sum of the voltages or currents produced by each independent source acting alone.
bullets: The circuit elements involved in the superposition argument must be linear. Resistors and the linear controlled sources used in this unit satisfy this condition.
When considering one independent voltage source, every other independent voltage source is set to zero. A zero-valued ideal voltage source is a short circuit.
When considering one independent current source, every other independent current source is set to zero. A zero-valued ideal current source is an open circuit.
Dependent/controlled sources are not deactivated because their values are determined by circuit variables; they remain part of every partial circuit.
The reference direction of the desired current or the reference polarity of the desired voltage must remain the same in every partial case so that signs are combined correctly.
steps: Identify the branch voltage or current to be found and mark its reference direction/polarity.
Keep the first independent source active and replace all other independent sources by their zero-valued equivalents.
Calculate the partial response produced by that source.
Repeat the procedure for every remaining independent source.
Add all partial responses algebraically. A negative partial value means that source acts opposite to the chosen reference direction/polarity.
paragraphs_after: The reason the theorem works is linearity: the circuit equations are linear in the source excitations and in the response variables, so the response to several excitations is the sum of the separate responses.

Superposition is applied directly to voltages and currents, not to power. Power expressions such as p = vi, i²R or v²/R are nonlinear. Therefore first obtain the total voltage or current by superposition and only then calculate power from that total response.
answer.note: A strong 6-mark answer should contain the statement, conditions, source-deactivation rules, step-by-step procedure, dependent-source rule and the power limitation.

questions.question: Discuss the DC response of an RL circuit and write the expression for transient current with respect to time.

paragraphs: Consider a series resistance \(R\) and inductance \(L\) connected at \(t=0\) to a constant DC voltage \(V\), with zero initial inductor current.
steps: KVL gives \(V=Ri+L\dfrac{di}{dt}\), or \(\dfrac{di}{dt}+\dfrac RL i=\dfrac VL\).
The complementary solution is \(i_c=Ce^{-Rt/L}\); a constant particular solution is \(i_p=V/R\). Hence \(i(t)=V/R+Ce^{-Rt/L}\).
Inductor current is continuous. Since \(i(0)=0\), \(C=-V/R\).
Therefore \(i(t)=\dfrac VR(1-e^{-t/\tau}),\quad\tau=L/R\). At \(t=\tau\), current is \((1-e^{-1})V/R\approx0.632V/R\).
The resistor voltage is \(v_R=V(1-e^{-t/\tau})\) and inductor voltage \(v_L=Ve^{-t/\tau}\). As \(t\to\infty\), current tends to \(V/R\) and the inductor voltage tends to zero.
For a nonzero initial current \(I_0\), the general response is \(i(t)=V/R+(I_0-V/R)e^{-t/\tau}\).
answer.result: \(i(t)=\dfrac VR(1-e^{-Rt/L}),\quad \tau=\dfrac LR\) for zero initial current.
answer.note: Supporting textbook material outside current R25 Unit I; now source-backed by the newly supplied pp.62–69.

2.title: Steady State AC Circuits
2.scope_note: The official Chapter 2 review page contains 17 questions: 11 short-answer (two-mark) and 6 essay (six-mark) questions. All are answerable from the supplied Unit II textbook pages 73–129 and the consolidated Unit II notes. Answers below are PankusDesk study solutions, not official textbook solutions.

questions.question: What are the advantages of a sinusoidal wave over other alternating waves?

bullets: Many alternating quantities can be represented as sums of sinusoidal components, making sinusoidal analysis broadly useful.
Sinusoidal signals are easy to generate and transmit.
They are mathematically convenient because differentiation and integration of a sinusoid produce another sinusoid.
In a linear circuit, a sinusoidal excitation gives a sinusoidal steady-state response at the same frequency, so analysis can focus on magnitude and phase.

questions.question: Define cycle and time period of an alternating quantity.

bullets: Cycle: one complete set of positive and negative values through which an alternating quantity passes before the waveform repeats.
Time period T: the time in seconds required to complete one cycle.
Frequency is related by f = 1/T.

questions.question: How do you represent the instantaneous value of an alternating quantity in terms of its maximum value and frequency?

paragraphs: For a sinusoidal quantity with zero initial phase, the instantaneous value is
paragraphs_after: If an initial phase φ is present, v(t) = V_m sin(2πft + φ).

questions.question: Show the voltage and current phasors in pure resistive, inductive and capacitive circuits.

rows: V and I are in phase

answer.note: For drawing, take current as reference: pure R has V along I; pure L has V vertically +90° from I; pure C has V vertically −90° from I.

questions.question: Find the phase angle between v = 250 sin(314t − 15°) and i = 10 sin(314t + 45°).

steps: Both quantities are already in sine form and have the same angular frequency.
Voltage phase = −15°.
Current phase = +45°.
Phase difference = 45° − (−15°) = 60°.
answer.book_check: This matches the printed answer of 60°.

questions.question: Define form factor and peak factor.

bullets: Form factor = RMS value / Average value.
Peak factor = Maximum (peak) value / RMS value.
For a sine wave, form factor ≈ 1.11 and peak factor = √2 ≈ 1.414.

questions.question: Express the phasor 8 − j6 in polar and exponential forms.

steps: Polar form = 10∠−36.87°.
Exponential form = 10e^(−j36.87°).
answer.book_check: Consistent with the printed check answer.

questions.question: Does a pure inductor consume active power? Why?

paragraphs: No. In a pure inductor, current lags voltage by 90°, so the power factor is cos90° = 0. Hence average active power P = VI cosφ = 0.

Instantaneous power alternates between positive and negative values as energy is stored in the magnetic field and then returned to the source. The net energy consumed over a complete cycle is therefore zero.

questions.question: Show the impedance triangle of a series RC circuit.

paragraphs: For a series RC circuit, Z = R − jX_C. In the impedance triangle, R is drawn horizontally to the right, X_C vertically downward, and |Z| is the hypotenuse joining the origin to the resultant.
answer.note: The downward reactive side represents the negative capacitive reactance; current leads the supply voltage.

questions.question: Differentiate between star and delta connections.

rows: Similar-polarity ends of three phases are joined to a common neutral/star point.
Dissimilar-polarity ends are connected to form a closed loop.
Neutral point is available in the basic star arrangement.
No neutral point in the basic delta arrangement.
Line voltage leads corresponding phase voltage by 30°.
Line current lags corresponding phase current by 30°.

questions.question: What is the phase difference between (i) any two phase voltages and (ii) any two line voltages in a balanced three-phase system?

bullets: Any two phase voltages are displaced by 120°.
Any two line voltages are also displaced by 120°.

questions.question: The maximum value of a sinusoidal alternating voltage of frequency 50 Hz is 300 V. Find the voltage at t = 5 ms, 10 ms and 12 ms.

paragraphs: For a zero-phase sinusoidal voltage, v(t) = V_m sinωt. Here V_m = 300 V and f = 50 Hz.
steps: At t = 10 ms = 0.010 s: angle = π, so v = 300 sinπ = 0 V.
answer.book_check: The printed check answer gives 300 V, 0 V and approximately −175.87 V; the small difference is rounding.

questions.question: Derive the expressions for average and RMS values of a sinusoidal alternating quantity.

paragraphs: Let the sinusoidal current be i = I_m sinθ. For a symmetrical sine wave, the algebraic average over one complete cycle is zero, so average magnitude is evaluated over a positive half cycle 0 ≤ θ ≤ π.
paragraphs_after: For RMS value, use the effective-value definition: square the instantaneous current, find its mean over the half cycle (equivalently a full cycle for i²), and take the square root.
steps: I_rms = √[(1/π)∫₀^π i² dθ].
Substitute i = I_m sinθ: I_rms = I_m√[(1/π)∫₀^π sin²θ dθ].
Use sin²θ = (1 − cos2θ)/2.
The integral of cos2θ over 0 to π is zero, leaving a mean value of 1/2.
Therefore I_rms = I_m/√2 = 0.707I_m.
answer.result: For a sine wave: Average over half cycle = 0.637 × peak; RMS = 0.707 × peak. The same derivation applies to voltage.
answer.note: For full marks, state why the half-cycle is used for average value and the heating/effective interpretation of RMS before the mathematics.

questions.question: Discuss the analysis of an AC circuit having a pure resistance and inductance in series.

paragraphs: Consider a resistor R and ideal inductor L connected in series across a sinusoidal AC supply. The same current I flows through both elements, so current is taken as the reference phasor.

The resistor voltage V_R = IR is in phase with current. The inductor voltage V_L = IX_L leads current by 90°, where X_L = 2πfL. Therefore the supply voltage is the phasor sum of these two perpendicular drops.
bullets: Current lags the applied voltage by angle φ, so the power factor is lagging.
Supply current: I = V/|Z|.
Voltage drops: V_R = IR and V_L = IX_L.
Active power: P = VI cosφ.
Reactive power: Q = VI sinφ.
Apparent power: S = VI = √(P² + Q²).
paragraphs_after: The phasor diagram is a right triangle with V_R along the current axis and V_L vertically +90°. The corresponding impedance triangle has R horizontally, X_L vertically and |Z| as the hypotenuse. A complete six-mark answer should include the circuit, phasor diagram, impedance triangle, phase relation and power expressions.

questions.question: Is there any possibility for a series RLC circuit to operate at unity power factor? Explain.

paragraphs: Yes. A series RLC circuit operates at unity power factor when its inductive and capacitive reactances are equal. The series impedance is
steps: For unity power factor, current and supply voltage must be in phase, so the net reactive component must be zero.
Set X_L − X_C = 0, hence X_L = X_C.
Using X_L = 2πfL and X_C = 1/(2πfC): 2πfL = 1/(2πfC).
Solving gives f_r = 1/(2π√LC).
bullets: At f = f_r, the circuit is in series resonance.
Net reactance is zero.
Impedance is minimum and equals R.
Current is I = V/R.
Phase angle φ = 0°.
Power factor cosφ = 1.
answer.result: A series RLC circuit has unity power factor at the resonant frequency, where X_L = X_C.
answer.note: R25 names series RLC analysis but not resonance as a separate topic; this condition is nevertheless explicitly developed in the prescribed chapter and is directly asked in its review questions.

questions.question: In a series RLC circuit, R = 6 Ω, L = 0.02 H and C = 300 μF are connected to a 230 V, 50 Hz AC supply. Find (i) supply current, (ii) voltage across each element and (iii) power-factor angle. Also draw the phasor diagram.

steps: Supply current I = V/|Z| = 230/7.40 ≈ 31.09 A.
Since X_C > X_L, the circuit is net capacitive and current leads the supply voltage.
Power-factor angle magnitude φ = tan⁻¹[(X_C − X_L)/R] = tan⁻¹(4.33/6) ≈ 35.8° leading.
answer.diagram: Take I as the horizontal reference. Draw V_R along I, V_L upward, V_C downward, and the supply voltage V as the vector from the origin to the resultant of V_R and (V_L − V_C). Because V_C > V_L, the resultant lies below the current axis.
answer.book_check: The printed current and element-voltage checks agree closely with these values. The review page prints 54.17° for the power-factor angle, but applying the chapter's own relation tanφ = |X_L − X_C|/R to the stated R, L, C and f gives about 35.8° leading. This discrepancy is retained explicitly rather than silently copied.

questions.question: Obtain the relation between phase and line values of voltage and current in a balanced three-phase delta-connected system.

paragraphs: In a balanced delta connection, each phase winding or load branch is connected directly between two line conductors. Therefore the voltage across each phase is the line-to-line voltage.
paragraphs_after: For current, consider one line junction. The line current is the phasor difference of the two equal phase currents meeting at that junction, for example I_A(line) = I_A − I_C. The two phase currents have equal magnitude I_ph and are 120° apart.
steps: Represent −I_C as a phasor opposite to I_C. The angle between I_A and −I_C is 60°.
By the parallelogram law: I_L² = I_ph² + I_ph² + 2I_ph² cos60°.
I_L² = 3I_ph².
Therefore I_L = √3I_ph.
The resultant line current is displaced by 30° from the corresponding phase current; in the delta connection shown, line current lags the corresponding phase current by 30°.
bullets: Voltage relation: V_L = V_ph.
Current relation: I_L = √3I_ph.
Line currents are mutually 120° apart.
Total balanced three-phase power can therefore be written P = √3V_LI_L cosφ.
answer.result: Balanced delta: V_L = V_ph and I_L = √3I_ph; line current lags the corresponding phase current by 30°.
answer.note: For full marks, include the delta connection and phasor diagram showing the phase-current difference that produces the line current.

questions.question: What is a transformer?

paragraphs: A transformer is a static electromagnetic device that transfers AC power from one circuit to another by mutual induction, normally changing voltage and current without changing frequency.

questions.question: List the uses of transformers.

paragraphs: Transformers step voltage up for economical transmission, step it down for distribution and utilisation, provide electrical isolation, and supply suitable voltages for electrical and electronic equipment.

questions.question: Write down the qualities of an ideal transformer.

paragraphs: An ideal transformer has zero winding resistance, no leakage flux, no hysteresis or eddy-current loss, and an infinitely permeable core requiring negligible magnetising current. Input power equals output power: efficiency is 100%.

questions.question: Differentiate between an ideal transformer and a practical transformer.

rows: Zero winding resistance; no copper loss
No core loss or magnetising current
Core loss and magnetising current exist

questions.question: Show the equivalent circuit of a transformer.

paragraphs: The complete circuit has primary winding resistance and leakage reactance, an exciting branch \(R_0\parallel jX_0\), an ideal transformer, and secondary winding resistance and leakage reactance. \(R_0\) represents core loss and \(X_0\) magnetisation. Impedances referred between sides change by the square of the turns ratio.

figures.alt: Figure 3.13 · Complete transformer equivalent circuit · Textbook p. 141

figures.figure_name: Equivalent circuit referred to secondary side
figures.alt: Figure 3.14 · Equivalent circuit referred to secondary side · Textbook p. 142

questions.question: Define voltage regulation.

paragraphs: In this chapter, transformer voltage regulation is the change in secondary terminal voltage from no-load to the specified load, expressed as a percentage of the no-load secondary EMF E₂, at unchanged primary voltage and frequency.
answer.note: This follows the supplied chapter’s no-load-voltage denominator. The approximate numerical method substitutes the rated secondary voltage for E₂.

questions.question: Specify the condition for maximum efficiency in a transformer.

paragraphs: At fixed power factor, efficiency is maximum when variable copper loss equals constant iron/core loss.

questions.question: The full-load copper losses of a transformer are 200 W. Find the copper losses at half full load.

steps: Copper loss varies as the square of load current: \(P_{\rm cu}(x)=x^2P_{\rm cu,FL}\).
At half load, \(x=0.5\), so \(P_{\rm cu}=0.5^2(200)=50\ \mathrm W\).

rows: Induced EMF drives the load current
Back EMF opposes the applied voltage
Fleming’s right-hand rule gives generated-current direction
Fleming’s left-hand rule gives force direction

questions.question: State Fleming’s right-hand rule.

paragraphs: Hold the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand mutually perpendicular. The forefinger points along the magnetic field (N to S), the thumb along conductor motion, and the middle finger gives the induced conventional current direction.

figures.alt: Figure 3.25 · Fleming’s right-hand rule · Textbook p. 160

questions.question: Show the circuit symbol of a DC generator.

paragraphs: The source symbol represents the generated EMF between the marked positive and negative terminals. In generator operation, load current leaves the positive terminal.

questions.question: Classify DC generators.

paragraphs: By excitation, DC generators are separately excited or self-excited. Self-excited generators are shunt, series or compound. Compound generators may be long-shunt or short-shunt, and cumulatively or differentially compounded.

questions.question: Why is back EMF called so?

paragraphs: Rotation of the armature in the magnetic field induces an EMF whose polarity opposes the voltage driving motor current, in accordance with Lenz’s law. It is therefore called back or counter EMF.

questions.question: State Fleming’s left-hand rule.

paragraphs: Hold the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular. The forefinger indicates field direction, the middle finger conventional current, and the thumb the force/motion of the conductor.

figures.alt: Figure 3.42 · Fleming’s left-hand rule · Textbook p. 172
Figure 3.43 · Fleming’s left-hand rule — conductor force · Textbook p. 172

questions.question: Show the torque versus armature-current characteristic of a DC separately excited motor.

paragraphs: With constant field excitation, \(T=k\phi I_a\). Thus torque is directly proportional to armature current, giving a straight line through the origin.

figures.alt: Figure 3.52 · Torque vs armature current characteristic · Textbook p. 179

questions.question: Explain the working principle of a transformer.

paragraphs: A transformer is a static device that transfers AC electrical power between circuits by mutual induction, normally changing voltage and current while retaining the supply frequency.
steps: Apply an alternating voltage to the primary winding. Its magnetising current establishes alternating flux in the common magnetic core.
This flux links both windings. Faraday’s law gives \(e_1=-N_1\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\) and \(e_2=-N_2\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\).
With the secondary open, the primary draws a small no-load current to establish flux and supply core losses. When a load is connected, the secondary EMF drives a load current.
The primary then draws an additional load component whose ampere-turns oppose the secondary ampere-turns, leaving the main flux approximately unchanged at fixed voltage and frequency.

Ideally, \(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}=\dfrac{N_2}{N_1}=k\) and \(\dfrac{I_2}{I_1}=\dfrac{1}{k}\). Thus a step-up transformer raises voltage and reduces current; a step-down transformer does the reverse. There is no conducting connection between isolated primary and secondary windings.

figures.alt: Figure 3.2 · Transformer principle · Textbook p. 131
Figure 3.3 · Transformer with an iron core · Textbook p. 131

questions.question: What are the main parts of a transformer? Explain briefly its construction.

paragraphs: The main parts are the magnetic core, insulated primary and secondary windings, and the insulation and cooling arrangements.
steps: Build the core from thin insulated magnetic-steel laminations. The core provides a low-reluctance path for common flux, while laminations reduce eddy-current loss.
Place insulated copper or aluminium primary and secondary windings on the core. The primary receives electrical power and the secondary supplies the load.
In core-type construction, the windings surround the core limbs; in shell-type construction, the core surrounds much of the winding. Maintain insulation between turns, windings and core.
Use a tank and insulating oil in oil-filled transformers, with cooling surfaces or radiators to remove winding and core heat. Bring out the terminals through insulated bushings.

figures.alt: Figure 3.4 · Basic construction of a transformer · Textbook p. 132

questions.question: Derive the EMF equation of a transformer.

paragraphs: Assume sinusoidal core flux \(\phi=\phi_m\sin\omega t\) at frequency \(f\).
steps: In one half-cycle the flux changes from \(+\phi_m\) to \(-\phi_m\), a magnitude change of \(2\phi_m\) in \(1/(2f)\) seconds.
Average induced EMF per turn is therefore \(\dfrac{2\phi_m}{1/(2f)}=4f\phi_m\).
For a sinusoidal waveform, form factor \(E_{\rm rms}/E_{\rm avg}=1.11\). Hence RMS EMF per turn is \(1.11(4f\phi_m)=4.44f\phi_m\).
Multiply by the number of turns: \(E_1=4.44fN_1\phi_m\) and \(E_2=4.44fN_2\phi_m\). Since \(\phi_m=B_mA\), also \(E=4.44fNB_mA\).
Dividing the two equations gives \(E_2/E_1=N_2/N_1\). Under the ideal-transformer assumption this is also \(V_2/V_1\).

figures.alt: Figure 3.5 · Transformer used for EMF-equation derivation · Textbook p. 133

questions.question: In a 110/440 V, 50 Hz single-phase transformer, the maximum flux density is 1.2 Wb/m² and the EMF per turn is 1.8 V. Determine (a) primary and secondary turns, (b) operating flux and (c) core cross-sectional area.

answer.book_check: The book gives approximately 61 and 245 turns, 8.12 mWb and 0.00676 m². The ideal turns above retain the given 1.8 V/turn without intermediate rounding; a physical winding requires integer turns.

parts.label: (a)
steps: Use RMS EMF per turn \(E_t=E/N=1.8\ \mathrm{V/turn}\). Neglect winding drops, so \(E_1=110\ \mathrm V\) and \(E_2=440\ \mathrm V\).
(a) \(N_1=110/1.8=61.11\) turns and \(N_2=440/1.8=244.44\) turns (ideal calculated values).

questions.question: A 25 kVA, 220/440 V, 50 Hz transformer has leakage impedance (0.2 + j0.55) Ω on the primary side and (0.8 + j2.4) Ω on the secondary side. Find percentage voltage regulation at ¾ full-load current supplying a resistive secondary load.

steps: The secondary-to-primary turns ratio is \(k=440/220=2\). Refer the primary impedance to the secondary by multiplying by \(k^2=4\).
Full-load secondary current \(I_{2,FL}=25000/440=56.818\ \mathrm A\). At ¾ load, \(I_2=0.75(56.818)=42.614\ \mathrm A\).

For a resistive load, \(\cos\phi=1,\ \sin\phi=0\). Using the chapter’s approximate voltage-drop formula with \(E_2\approx440\ \mathrm V\): \(\%\mathrm{VR}\approx\dfrac{I_2(R_{02}\cos\phi+X_{02}\sin\phi)}{E_2}\,100=\dfrac{42.614(1.6)}{440}\,100\).
answer.book_check: Book answer: 15.49%, agreeing within rounding. This uses the prescribed approximate voltage-drop formula.

questions.question: A 20 kVA, 400/200 V, 50 Hz transformer has primary resistance 48 mΩ and secondary resistance 18 mΩ. Iron losses are 200 W. Find efficiency at half full load and 0.8 power factor lagging.

steps: Half-load copper loss \(P_{cu}=0.5^2(300)=75\ \mathrm W\). Core loss remains \(P_i=200\ \mathrm W\).
answer.book_check: Book answer: 96.67%; the difference is rounding.

questions.question: With a neat sketch, explain the operation of a DC generator (simple loop generator).

paragraphs: A DC generator converts mechanical power into electrical power using electromagnetic induction. A simple loop generator illustrates the operation.
steps: Rotate a coil mechanically between north and south magnetic poles. The two active sides cut magnetic flux and induced EMFs appear along them.
Use Fleming’s right-hand rule to obtain each conductor’s induced current direction. The coil-side EMFs add around the loop.
After each half-turn, the direction in which each side cuts flux reverses, so the EMF within the rotating coil alternates.
Connect the coil ends to a split-ring commutator and stationary brushes. Every half-turn the commutator reverses the coil-to-brush connection at the same time as the coil EMF reverses.

The external brush polarity therefore remains unchanged: a single coil gives pulsating unidirectional voltage, and many coils/commutator segments make it smoother. Mechanical input supplies the load power and losses.

figures.alt: Figure 3.26 · Simple loop generator · Textbook p. 161
Figure 3.28 · Commutator · Textbook p. 162
Figure 3.29 · Action of commutator · Textbook p. 162
Figure 3.30 · Unidirectional or direct current · Textbook p. 163

questions.question: Briefly explain the constructional aspects of a DC machine.

paragraphs: The same basic DC-machine construction can operate as a motor or a generator.
steps: Yoke: provides mechanical support and the return path for magnetic flux. Main poles and pole shoes support the field coils and spread flux over the armature.
Field winding: produces the main magnetic field when excited by DC.
Armature core: a laminated rotating iron cylinder with slots; laminations reduce eddy-current loss. Armature conductors occupy the slots and form the armature winding.
Commutator: insulated copper segments connected to armature coils; it mechanically rectifies the internally alternating generated EMF in generator operation.
Brushes: stationary carbon contacts collect or supply current through the rotating commutator. The shaft, bearings and end covers support rotation.

figures.figure_name: Basic construction of a DC machine
figures.alt: Figure 3.31 · Basic construction of a DC machine · Textbook p. 163

questions.question: Derive the expression for EMF generated in a DC generator.

paragraphs: Let \(P\) be the pole number, \(\phi\) flux per pole in webers, \(Z\) total armature conductors, \(N\) speed in rpm and \(A\) parallel armature paths.
steps: In one revolution a conductor cuts the flux of all poles: total flux cut \(=P\phi\) webers.
Time per revolution is \(60/N\) seconds. Average induced EMF per conductor is \(\dfrac{P\phi}{60/N}=\dfrac{P\phi N}{60}\).
There are \(Z/A\) series conductors in each parallel path. The brush-to-brush EMF equals the EMF of one such path.
Thus \(E_g=\dfrac{P\phi N}{60}\dfrac{Z}{A}\). For simplex lap winding \(A=P\); for simplex wave winding \(A=2\).

figures.figure_name: Conductor passing through a pole pitch
figures.alt: Figure 3.35 · Conductor passing through a pole pitch · Textbook p. 166

questions.question: A four-pole lap-connected DC motor with 1000 armature conductors absorbs 25 A from a DC source. Flux per pole is 24 mWb. Find the supply voltage needed for 1500 rpm if armature resistance is 0.8 Ω and brush drop is 2 V.

steps: For simplex lap winding \(A=P=4\). Use \(\phi=24\times10^{-3}=0.024\ \mathrm{Wb}\) and take the stated current as armature current \(I_a=25\ \mathrm A\).
For motor operation, supply must overcome back EMF, resistance drop and brush drop: \(V=E_b+I_aR_a+V_{brush}=600+25(0.8)+2\).

questions.question: Explain the operating characteristics of a separately excited DC motor.

paragraphs: In a separately excited DC motor, an independent DC supply energises the field. With field excitation fixed, flux \(\phi\) is approximately constant.
steps: Torque is \(T\propto\phi I_a\). At constant flux, \(T\propto I_a\), so the torque–armature-current characteristic is a straight line through the origin.
Back EMF satisfies \(E_b=V-I_aR_a\) when brush drop is neglected. Since \(E_b\propto\phi N\), speed is \(N\propto\dfrac{V-I_aR_a}{\phi}\).
As armature current increases, \(I_aR_a\) increases and speed falls slightly at constant terminal voltage and flux. The speed–current curve therefore has a small negative slope.
Because torque is proportional to armature current, the speed–torque curve also falls gently as torque rises. This gives approximately constant-speed operation over the normal load range.

figures.alt: Figure 3.51 · Separately excited DC motor · Textbook p. 178
Figure 3.52 · Torque vs armature current characteristic · Textbook p. 179
Figure 3.53 · Speed vs armature current characteristic · Textbook p. 180
Figure 3.54 · Speed vs torque characteristic · Textbook p. 180

questions.question: What methods control the speed of a separately excited DC motor? Explain briefly.

paragraphs: The governing relation is \(N\propto\dfrac{V_a-I_aR_a}{\phi}\). The textbook describes field control and armature-voltage control.
steps: Field control: keep armature voltage approximately constant and insert a variable resistance in the separately supplied field circuit.

Increasing field resistance reduces field current and flux. Since speed is inversely proportional to flux, speed increases. Field weakening is normally used above base/rated speed; reduced flux also reduces torque per ampere.
Armature-voltage control: hold field current and flux constant and vary the voltage supplied to the armature.
Reducing armature voltage reduces back EMF and speed. This gives smooth control below base/rated speed; the approximately straight speed–voltage characteristic follows from the governing relation.

figures.alt: Figure 3.56 · Field control method · Textbook p. 182
Figure 3.57 · Field current vs speed characteristic · Textbook p. 182
Figure 3.58 · Armature control method · Textbook p. 183
Figure 3.59 · Armature voltage vs speed characteristic · Textbook p. 184

questions.question: Name the different parts of an induction motor.

paragraphs: The main parts are the stator frame, laminated stator core and three-phase winding; the rotor (squirrel-cage or wound/slip-ring type); air gap; shaft, bearings, end covers and cooling fan.

questions.question: Why is an induction motor called an asynchronous motor?

paragraphs: Its rotor runs at a speed different from the synchronous speed of the rotating stator field. Normal motor operation requires positive slip; without relative motion, no rotor EMF and torque are induced.

questions.question: Define slip.

paragraphs: Slip is the difference between synchronous speed and rotor speed, divided by synchronous speed.

questions.question: Define synchronous speed.

paragraphs: Synchronous speed is the rotational speed of the stator magnetic field.
answer.result: \(N_s=\dfrac{120f}{P}\ \mathrm{rpm}\), where \(f\) is supply frequency in Hz and \(P\) is the number of poles.

questions.question: What are the values of slip (a) at starting and (b) at synchronous speed?

parts.label: (a)
steps: At starting \(N=0\): \(s=(N_s-0)/N_s=1\).

parts.label: (b)
steps: At synchronous speed \(N=N_s\): \(s=0\).

questions.question: Explain the constructional aspects of squirrel-cage and slip-ring induction motors.

paragraphs: A three-phase induction motor has a stationary stator and a rotating rotor separated by a small air gap.
steps: The outer stator frame supports a laminated steel core with slots carrying a distributed three-phase winding. The phase windings are displaced by 120 electrical degrees.
A squirrel-cage rotor has conducting bars in slots, short-circuited by end rings. Bars are usually skewed; there are no external rotor terminals, making it robust and simple.
A phase-wound/slip-ring rotor carries an insulated three-phase winding, normally star-connected. Its free ends connect to slip rings and brushes.
External rotor resistances can be inserted through slip rings for starting or control and then removed/shorted during normal running. Shaft, bearings and cooling arrangements complete the machine.

Figure 4.3 · Slip-ring induction motor · Textbook p. 187
Figure 4.4 · Squirrel-cage rotor · Textbook p. 188

questions.question: Explain the working of a three-phase induction motor.

paragraphs: A three-phase induction motor operates by electromagnetic induction and the interaction of the rotating stator field with rotor currents.
steps: Balanced three-phase stator currents in windings displaced by 120 electrical degrees create a resultant magnetic field of nearly constant magnitude rotating at \(N_s=120f/P\) rpm.
The rotating field sweeps past the initially stationary rotor conductors. The resulting flux cutting induces rotor EMF; the closed rotor circuit allows current to flow.
Interaction of rotor current with the magnetic field produces electromagnetic torque. By Lenz’s law, the rotor turns in the field’s direction to reduce relative motion.
The rotor must lag the field under motoring load. At \(N=N_s\) there is no relative motion, induced rotor EMF or sustained torque.
Slip is \(s=(N_s-N)/N_s\), rotor frequency \(f_r=sf\), rotor EMF \(E_{2s}=sE_2\) and rotor reactance \(X_{2s}=sX_2\).

figures.alt: Figure 4.5 · Three-phase supply and stator winding · Textbook p. 189
Figure 4.6 · Production of rotating magnetic field · Textbook p. 189
Figure 4.7 · Stator and rotor fluxes · Textbook p. 189

questions.question: Show and explain the torque–slip characteristics of a three-phase induction motor. Identify its maximum and starting torque.

paragraphs: For a given supply and approximately constant air-gap flux, induction-motor torque varies with slip as \(T\propto\dfrac{sR_2}{R_2^2+(sX_2)^2}\).
steps: At synchronous speed \(s=0\), so induced rotor current and torque are zero.
At small slip, \(sX_2\ll R_2\) and torque is approximately proportional to slip: \(T\propto s\). This is the normal stable motoring region.
Torque reaches its maximum when \(R_2=s_mX_2\), or \(s_m=R_2/X_2\) under the textbook simplified model.
Beyond maximum torque, the reactance term dominates and \(T\propto1/s\). At standstill \(s=1\) the curve gives starting torque.

Increasing rotor resistance moves the maximum-torque point toward higher slip, without changing its approximate magnitude at the same supply. This explains improved starting torque with external rotor resistance.

figures.alt: Figure 4.9 · Torque-slip characteristics · Textbook p. 196

questions.question: Explain the working of a synchronous generator.

paragraphs: A synchronous generator (alternator) converts mechanical power into AC electrical power.
steps: Provide a DC-excited rotor field and a three-phase armature winding on the stator. The stator phase windings are displaced by 120 electrical degrees.
A prime mover rotates the rotor field. Its moving magnetic flux links each stationary stator winding.
By Faraday’s law, the changing linkage induces alternating EMFs. The spatial phase displacement makes the three phase EMFs 120 electrical degrees apart.
For \(P\) poles rotating at \(N\) rpm, each revolution produces \(P/2\) cycles. Hence \(f=PN/120\) and \(N_s=120f/P\).
When a load is connected, current flows through the stator and electrical power is delivered. The prime mover must supply the corresponding mechanical input plus losses.

figures.alt: Figure 4.10 · Synchronous-generator block diagram · Textbook p. 197
Figure 4.11 · Cross-sectional view of synchronous machine · Textbook p. 198
Figure 4.12 · Sinusoidal generated voltage · Textbook p. 198

questions.question: Discuss the working of a stepper motor.

paragraphs: A stepper motor converts a sequence of electrical pulses into discrete angular movements. Each pulse advances the rotor by a fixed step angle.
steps: Energise one stator phase or phase group. The rotor aligns with the resulting magnetic field (or minimum-reluctance position for a reluctance rotor).
Switch excitation to the next phase in the prescribed sequence. The stator-field axis changes position and the rotor moves by one step to the next stable alignment.
Repeat the phase sequence to obtain continuous stepped rotation. Reverse the excitation sequence to reverse rotation.
For \(n\) input pulses and step angle \(\alpha\), angular displacement is \(\theta=n\alpha\). Pulse frequency controls speed and pulse count controls position.
Applications include printers, plotters, robotics, CNC/positioning systems and other digital motion-control mechanisms.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a fuse? Show its symbol.

paragraphs: A fuse is an overcurrent protective element connected in series with the circuit. Excess current heats and melts the fuse element, opening the circuit. It protects against excessive current; it is not a general detector of every earth-leakage fault.

questions.question: Why is earthing of electrical appliances done?

paragraphs: Earthing connects exposed metal bodies to a low-resistance protective path so that an insulation fault does not leave the body dangerously live. It limits touch voltage and allows protective devices to disconnect the faulty circuit.

questions.question: Name the different types of earthing.

paragraphs: The chapter lists plate earthing, pipe earthing, rod earthing and strip/wire earthing. Pipe and plate earthing are the two methods developed in the current R25 unit.

questions.question: Mention the purpose of providing charcoal and salt in earth pits.

paragraphs: In the traditional textbook earthing arrangement, charcoal and salt around the electrode help retain moisture and improve soil contact/conductivity, reducing electrode-to-earth resistance.

questions.question: Differentiate between primary and secondary batteries.

rows: Designed for one discharge cycle; not normally recharged
Reversible electrochemical reaction permits repeated recharging
Replace after useful charge is exhausted
Recharge with an appropriate external source

questions.question: What are the units for electrical energy consumption?

paragraphs: The SI unit of energy is the joule. Commercial electrical energy is usually measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), called units.

questions.question: Show the basic layout of wiring in a domestic installation and locate the energy meter, MCB and distribution board (DB).

paragraphs: A domestic installation distributes the incoming supply to lighting, socket and power circuits, with isolation, overload/short-circuit protection and protective earthing.
steps: Trace the incoming service through the supplier’s cut-out/service fuse and energy meter to the consumer main switch and distribution board (DB). The energy meter measures consumption; it is not a protective device.
The main switch provides installation isolation. The DB contains the outgoing protective devices, with separate MCB-protected final circuits for lighting and socket/power loads.
Connect loads in parallel so each receives the supply voltage and can be controlled independently. Put the ordinary single-pole switches and overcurrent protective devices in the live conductors.
Keep the neutral distribution and protective-earth system distinct. Connect exposed metal appliance bodies to the protective-earth conductor and electrode system.
Identify the energy meter before the consumer main distribution, the DB near the main switch, and the outgoing MCBs at the DB as labelled in the supplied layout.

questions.question: Discuss the merits and demerits of cleat and conduit wiring systems.

paragraphs: Cleat wiring carries insulated conductors on cleats; conduit wiring carries insulated conductors inside protective tubes.

rows: Low cost; quick installation and removal; easy inspection and alteration
Exposed to mechanical/weather damage; unattractive; mainly temporary service
Good mechanical protection; durable; neat when concealed; suitable for permanent installation
Higher initial cost; skilled labour; alterations and fault location can be difficult, especially when concealed

questions.question: List the differences between MCB and MCCB.

paragraphs: Both devices interrupt overcurrent, but their application ranges and construction differ.

rows: Usually fixed for the chosen rating and characteristic
Thermal overload and magnetic short-circuit trip in typical devices
Thermal-magnetic or electronic overcurrent trip, depending on design

questions.question: Show and explain the pipe-earthing scheme.

paragraphs: Earthing connects exposed conducting metal parts to the general mass of earth through a low-resistance path. It limits touch voltage and enables protective disconnection under a fault.
steps: Install the perforated galvanised-iron pipe electrode vertically in the ground as shown in the source figure, at a location where effective contact with moist soil can be maintained.
Pack the surrounding region with the specified alternating charcoal and salt layers to lower contact resistance in the traditional textbook arrangement.
Clamp the earth lead securely to the electrode and connect it to the installation’s protective-earthing terminal and exposed appliance bodies.
Provide the source’s watering/funnel and inspection arrangement to maintain and inspect the electrode connection.

During an insulation failure, the earth conductor provides a fault-current path; the protective device must disconnect the faulty circuit. Earthing is used together with protection, not as permission to touch live parts.

questions.question: Explain the working of a lead-acid battery.

paragraphs: A lead-acid cell is a rechargeable (secondary) cell. It has positive lead-dioxide plates, negative spongy-lead plates, dilute sulphuric-acid electrolyte, separators and a suitable container.
steps: On discharge, both plate materials convert to lead sulphate while sulphuric acid is consumed and water forms. Electrons flow through the external load from the negative plate to the positive plate.
The overall discharge reaction is \(\mathrm{Pb+PbO_2+2H_2SO_4\longrightarrow2PbSO_4+2H_2O}\). Electrolyte specific gravity and terminal voltage decrease.

Apply a suitable external DC charging source of correct polarity. Charging reverses the reaction: \(\mathrm{2PbSO_4+2H_2O\longrightarrow Pb+PbO_2+2H_2SO_4}\). The plate materials and acid concentration are restored.
A lead-acid cell has nominal voltage about 2 V. Multiple cells in series provide the required battery voltage.

Capacity is expressed in ampere-hours: \(C=It\) for constant discharge current. Available capacity depends on discharge rate and operating conditions. The supplied voltage and capacity curves illustrate this dependence.

questions.question: A 7.5 HP, three-phase, 400 V induction-motor drive operates for 4 hours daily at ¾ full load. Its efficiency is 80% at ¾ full load. Calculate monthly electrical energy consumption in kWh and the cost at ₹6.50 per unit.

paragraphs: Take a 30-day month, as in the printed answer, and \(1\ \mathrm{HP}=746\ \mathrm W\). The HP rating is mechanical full-load output; the energy meter records electrical input.
steps: Full-load output \(P_{FL}=7.5(746)=5595\ \mathrm W\). At ¾ load, \(P_o=0.75(5595)=4196.25\ \mathrm W\).
Electrical input \(P_i=P_o/\eta=4196.25/0.80=5245.3125\ \mathrm W=5.2453125\ \mathrm{kW}\).
Running time \(t=4(30)=120\ \mathrm h\). Energy \(E=5.2453125(120)=629.4375\ \mathrm{kWh}\).
Charge \(=629.4375(6.50)=4091.34375\) rupees. The 400 V rating is not needed because output power and efficiency already determine input power.

math_mismatch.label: Textbook answer discrepancy
math_mismatch.message: The book prints “620 units or KWH, Rs 4034/-”. With 7.5 HP, ¾ load, 80% efficiency, 4 hours per day and a 30-day month, the result is 629.4375 kWh and ₹4091.34 using 746 W/HP. The printed energy and price also do not agree with each other at ₹6.50 per unit. Month length is not stated in the question; for d days, energy is 20.98125d kWh and the charge is ₹136.378125d.

questions.question: Show the block diagram of a typical uninterruptible power supply (UPS) and briefly explain its operation.

paragraphs: A UPS maintains an AC supply to its load when the normal AC source fails, using energy stored in a battery.
steps: The AC input feeds a rectifier/charger, which converts AC to DC and charges the battery. The DC bus supplies the inverter.
The inverter converts the DC supply into AC suitable for the protected load. The battery is connected to support the DC bus.
During a mains failure, battery energy continues to feed the inverter, which supplies the load for the available backup duration.
When the mains returns, the normal source resumes operation and the charger replenishes the battery. Backup time depends on usable battery energy, load demand and conversion losses.
Read the power paths in the supplied Figure 5.44. Transfer/bypass behaviour depends on the UPS topology; the diagram is not a claim that every UPS type has an identical switching arrangement.
